analysis.one_liner: Cancels private student loans when a borrower dies or becomes disabled, shielding cosigners.
analysis.headline: A bill to erase private student loan debt when a borrower dies or becomes disabled — with 5 Democratic Senate sponsors — died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Christopher's Law would have required private student loan lenders to cancel the debt of a borrower, their estate, and any cosigner when the borrower dies or becomes permanently disabled. It also would bar lenders from punishing a borrower for a cosigner's death or bankruptcy, set rules for releasing cosigners from loans, extend federal parent loan cancellation when a student becomes disabled, and apply to loans already outstanding.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers with private student loans who die or become permanently disabled, their estates, and their cosigners — mostly parents and relatives who would otherwise remain legally on the hook for the debt. Per the bill's own findings, more than 90% of new private student loans are cosigned, and lenders release fewer than 1% of eligible cosigners. Parent borrowers of federal PLUS loans also gain if their child becomes disabled.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cosigners of private student loans, mostly parents

how_it_helps.text: Requires private lenders to discharge the loan — freeing the borrower, the borrower's estate, and any cosigner from repaying principal and interest — when the borrower dies, becomes disabled, or cannot work [S2].

Bars lenders from declaring a default, accelerating the debt, or raising the interest rate against a borrower because a cosigner died, became disabled, or went bankrupt — and bars action against a cosigner because the borrower went bankrupt [S3].

Requires the consumer bureau to set criteria forcing automatic cosigner release for borrowers who meet them, after the bill's findings noted lenders give cosigner release to fewer than 1% of eligible borrowers, and requires lenders to disclose release criteria up front and not tighten them later without the borrower's consent [S3].
Extends cancellation of federal parent loans to cases where the student — not just the parent — dies or becomes permanently disabled, applying retroactively to existing loans [S3].
Lets borrowers designate a trusted person to act on their behalf on the loan if they die or become disabled, and requires lenders to explain cosigner obligations in plain terms at signing [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private student loan lenders would absorb the losses on every loan they must discharge, including loans already made, since the bill applies to outstanding debt regardless of when the death, disability, or bankruptcy occurred. Some of that cost could be passed forward to future student borrowers through higher rates or tighter credit standards.

drawbacks.text: The discharge requirement applies retroactively to every outstanding private loan, regardless of when the loan was made or the death or disability occurred, so lenders would take losses on risk they priced years earlier — a cost some would likely recover through higher rates or less credit for future students [S3].

Relief hinges on meeting the federal definition of death, disability, or inability to work, which the bill ties to Education Department standards and requires anti-fraud safeguards, meaning borrowers and families would still have to navigate a government determination process to qualify [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted: it stops lenders and debt collectors from pursuing grieving parents and estates over a child's student debt, a practice the CFPB complaint record cited in the bill documented. The main cost falls on lenders, and the retroactive application to existing loans is aggressive — but the amounts at stake are debts that, in the death and disability cases the bill targets, families had no realistic way to escape. On balance the protections outweigh the pass-through pricing risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate's education committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Menendez introduced Christopher's Law on July 31, 2019, joined by Senators Booker, Warren, Brown, and Gillibrand [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student loan lenders, which can continue collecting on loans from cosigners and estates when a borrower dies or becomes disabled.

for.name: Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its case for discharging loans when borrowers die or become disabled.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (chaired by Sen. Lamar Alexander)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 31, 2019 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died there [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All five Senate sponsors were Democrats; the Republican-chaired committee of jurisdiction took no action, and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: The bill would force lenders to write off loans when borrowers die or become disabled — including loans already on their books — and would end practices like automatic defaults and cosigner releases granted to under 1% of eligible borrowers. Their gain from the bill's failure is continuing to collect from cosigners and estates.

industries.industry: Student loan debt collectors and servicers
industries.note: Discharge on death or disability would remove accounts that collectors and servicers pursue against cosigners and estates after a borrower's death or disability.
